utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that the Defence would like to go into private session to address a certain matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before going into private session, I've got just a couple of shortish points to address in open session. Your Honour, first of all, it's this: The Trial Chamber is continuing with Mr. Vasic's evidence this morning. We hope, of course, that won't take too long, whatever "too long" is, and then we have a witness, not protected. We have a witness, Mr. Divcic, coming afterwards. Your Honour, we have, and of course we have been in frequent communication with the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution as well at the same time, about the arrangements for witnesses. We have done our best, and we had intended and attempted to have another witness ready this week to follow on Mr. Divcic whenever he might finish. Of course, we don't know exactly when that might be and how much of this four-day week would be left. But Your Honour, the position is we have simply been unable to find a witness who meets all the necessary criteria to be here, including such matters as having the travel documents and of course the time available and so on. So, Your Honour, with the assurance that we have really tried hard and we have been doing our best on that, that is the position, Your Honour. The witnesses, the only witnesses that are available this week are Mr. Vasic continuing and then Mr. Divcic, where that ends up as a matter of timing, of course, is slightly unpredictable. So that's the first point. The second point, Your Honour, is that I did at the very end of the sessions before we had the recent break, I did indicate a couple of difficulties to the Trial Chamber as the Defence saw it in relation to the timetabling and the scheduling. We have had no response from Your Honours in relation to that. I just wish, therefore, to make it clear, Your Honour, those difficulties do not go away, and in particular, when we made our application for an extension of time to file the various material in relation to 65 ter, I set out, intending to be helpful, I set out in some detail a number of calls on the time of the Defence team, and specifically a number of calls on my time. Your Honours, those calls have not gone away. Matters on that list, which are absolutely essential, remain undone. They have to be done. They have to be fitted in. I cannot be in two places at once and I cannot -- well, I can do two things at once, but I can't do two major tasks at once. I have to deal with some of these long postponed, important management issues and financial issues, and I cannot do all the normal trial work at the same time. And some of those matters on that list have to have my immediate priority and will have my immediate priority. And I therefore, leaving aside the medium and longer-term issues of timing, I have to stress that, Your Honour. And there is only so much that I can ask my co-counsel to do, and he does beyond the call of duty anyway, as on many occasions I had to ask my previous co-counsel to do. And I do wish to stress that, Your Honour. This is a very oppressive burden that is being imposed on this team, and that has not changed. And I don't know whether we were going to receive any reaction or feedback whatever from the Trial Chamber in relation to the concerns which I expressed about ten days ago. The third point is just this, Your Honour: Mr. Krajisnik has a few matters which at some point he is particularly concerned to raise with the Trial Chamber. They're not, let me say, directly related to the immediate course of the trial, but they are matters, and I've spoken to Mr. Krajisnik, they are matters which he has agreed, we have agreed, that he and I should discuss first before we trouble the Trial Chamber any further. But it is likely that at some point quite soon Mr. Krajisnik will want to raise matters. Whether the Trial Chamber then wishes to take them any further, well, we'll see when -- as and when they are raised. So, Your Honour, that's all I have to say this morning, unless Your Honours have any questions to put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You raised three points. The first one, we just take notice of it at this time. We can't do anything else. But of course, there might come a point where -- well, let me not say anything prior to having discussed it thoroughly with my colleagues. The same is true for the second issue you raised. The third and the first are related to the extent that if there's something to be raised that -- well, the first point might create some additional time this week to raise any issue if we have no witnesses anymore, then at least we could use our time to hear what Mr. Krajisnik would like to submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I doubt very much in fact whether those points I mentioned at the end will take very long, but then one often says that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then at least we are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at this point that the Defence would request going into private session for Mr. Josse to deal with something that arose at the end of the week before last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Divcic again in fact yesterday evening, and unfortunately, he told me that he had ended up bumping into Mr. Vasic. I'm bound to observe in passing, it's rather unfortunate that they were both placed in the same hotel. I'm not going to be in any way critical of the VWS, because we've asked for our witnesses to stay at this particular hotel in terms of our own liaison. Having said that, of course, we don't need to liaise. In fact, we can't liaise with Mr. Vasic at this particular juncture. I should say also one other thing by way of preamble. I had a meeting with Mr. Margetts and Mr. Tieger in order to agree a formula to be sent to Mr. Vasic to request more documents from him. That was done via the victims and witnesses service. Exactly what has happened, I don't know, and I very much doubt that Mr. Tieger knows either, because effectively Mr. Margetts sent the document to the VWS, and we were reliant upon them to convey the information to Mr. Vasic. The point I'm coming to is this: Mr. Vasic handed to Mr. Divcic some documents. Mr. Divcic brought them, in a rather embarrassed fashion, to be fair to Mr. Divcic, to our meeting, and I've handed them to Mr. Karganovic. I don't think -- well, he hasn't yet told me what they say. They in fact contain a few English documents. So those I understand. It may be that before my learned friend concludes the cross-examination, he'd like to know a little more about this. Clearly I'll need to know a little more about it from Mr. Karganovic when he's translated the documents. But I just thought I should put that on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's essentially an accurate summary of what transpired at the end of last week, and of course my learned friend is quite right. We, number one, don't know what action, if any, was taken in response to the communication sent by the Victims and Witnesses Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the two documents the witnesses was invited to bring with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So we certainly would invite the Court to inquire and find out what the status is at this point, and if the documents that were provided -- that are now in the hands of Mr. Karganovic via Mr. Divcic are different, we would also like to know what those documents are about. So we're in the Court's hands at this point and we know nothing more than has just been explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible to hear from the Defence, well, let's say, at the first break, what approximately is the type of documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly. They're not very voluminous. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Then, if there's no other procedural issue to be raised, we'd like to invite Madam Usher to bring Mr. Vasic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic. Please be seated. First of all, thank you very much for returning to The Hague, Mr. Vasic. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony some two weeks ago, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Is that clear that that's still binding upon you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to continue your cross-examination, I'd like to ask you: Did you receive a request from the Victims and Witness Unit to bring some documents with you upon your new appearance in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the request last night, so all I managed to do was receive a copy of one document through the hotel fax, but I still haven't managed to get the second one. Because I wasn't told about this before I left home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That needs some further inquiries into the communications between Victims and Witness Section and this witness, not to say to blame anyone at this moment, but at least to find out what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll take that upon myself, simply because Mr. Vasic was a Defence witness. I'll speak to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us which documents you were able to obtain through this telefax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said last time that it would be a good idea if I could provide papers from the Municipal Assembly, not just the meeting on the 14th of August, but others as well, and so I asked the people I knew and they tried to put it into a smaller format, and so here you have the list of attendants for both 1992 and 1993, and you can see that Muslims attendance was actually higher, and that goes for Croats, of course, and there were more of them on later occasions than on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course we can't see anything yet, because we have not seen the document. Would you please be so kind to give the copies --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I also have the complete set of minutes from the two subsequent meetings between the one on the 14th of August and the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please provide them to Madam Usher so that they'll be put in the hands of Mr. Registrar, who can take care that they'll be copied for the parties. Then another question I'd like to raise, Mr. Vasic: Did you have any contact with other witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just heard that another witness has arrived who is supposed to give evidence. I was told what his name was. I couldn't remember it. But at dinner I saw him across the room and then we simply shook hands in the presence of one of your officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you had no conversation with him, apart from just saying hello.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few words, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just courtesy, nothing else, just hello and "I'm from..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the usual. He said: "I haven't seen you for two years," and I said that I couldn't remember his name at first. I said what used to be your job, and then he said he was at Pale and that during the war he was working for an organisation called Dobrotvor. And the thing is, we couldn't have easy communication between Prnjavor and Pale back then. And then I asked him where he was working now, and he said he's working for the electricity board at the moment. That's all. And then I said that I'm a businessman now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No exchange of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask Madam Usher to escort the witness for one second out of the courtroom and to remain standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I just want to be sure that I make no mistake and that I did not misunderstand anything at all. From what you said earlier, I did understand that Mr. Divcic gave you some documents that he said to have received from Mr. Vasic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what I understood the position to be, Your Honour. Could Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, no secret about this, speaks a little bit of English, so there have been times I communicate directly with him, but for the most part, it's been through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karganovic did translate that conversation for me, and that is what we remember Mr. Divcic to have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any preference on whether the Chamber would deal with it or would you make that part of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're content for the Chamber to deal with it directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I intend to confront the witness with the information we received and the answer he's given to my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me two minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just so that -- because I think Mr. Karganovic had looked at these documents. It might help everyone if we know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even if they were the same, my question was simply whether there was any exchange of documents. I mean, even if it's the same, it shouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give you your two minutes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have now, Your Honour - excuse me - have some vague idea what these documents are about. I'm going to hand them to Your Honour, simply because if Your Honour is going to embark on this sort of exercise, and I say I couldn't possibly object to that, ultimately it might help if you're able to present the witness with the documents. That's what I would want to do if I was cross-examining him in this way. There are a couple of English-language documents, one from a deputy High Representative, which just speaks for itself, at the bottom of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one handwritten document among the documents. Is Mr. Karganovic in a position to tell us approximately what it is? It turns out that all the other documents seem to be contemporaneous documents rather than documents from the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's unclear, and perhaps we should go into private session for one moment, to see whether Mr. Karganovic could help us out to identify what this handwritten document approximately is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, please be seated. I asked you whether, when you met Mr. Divcic, whether you exchanged any documents. Your answer was no. Is that still your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me whether I handed over to the other witness any documents. I did not hand him over any documents for him, but I gave him an envelope for the Defence, since he was saying that he was going to a meeting with the Defence team. But it was not any documents for him personally. It was just for the Defence team. And so I gave it to him to take to the Defence team. And some of the evidence that you asked for was placed in that envelope. So it was for the Defence team. It wasn't for him. Because I thought that since I was under oath, I shouldn't give anything to him personally. And that's the way I understood your question. Did I give him any documents for himself? I didn't. So there must have been a misunderstanding. And this envelope that I provided here, and another sheet of paper that is in the same envelope, was handed over to the Defence. This was the request that was made. And I had no other communication with the Defence team. And he just simply told me that he was going to meet with the Defence team, and I asked him to take that to them. But I wasn't giving it to him for any reason, nor would it be useful to him. It's just the attendance list for those meetings, plus a kind of acknowledgment that I received. So yeah, that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask you whether you gave him any documents for his personal use. I just asked you whether you gave him any documents. The answer should have been "yes, I did," and then you could have given the explanation you just gave. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not 100 per cent sure. I seem to remember that you asked, had I given any documents to the witness. I can't claim with a great deal of certainty, but I seem to remember that that was the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read to you exactly what I said. My question was: "No exchange of documents?" Perfectly neutral. Your answer was: "No." Your answer should have been: "Yes. I gave him an envelope, not for his personal use, but in order to give this to the Defence team." It also means that you at least discussed, that appears from your answer, that he would have a further discussion with the Defence team, which is different from what you told us before, that is, that you just exchanged information like "I haven't seen you, I don't remember your name." Then finally, didn't I instruct you not to speak with anyone, including Defence, about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question to mean, and I might have misunderstood, whether I gave him any documents for his own use. And the waitress at the hotel, or rather, not the waitress, but the official who was taking care of us at the hotel, said to me, "Okay, there's another witness and you might see him at dinner," and that was the way it was. Perhaps for another five minutes, that person stayed there for about two or three minutes, so I didn't feel it was a problem. Because there was an official from the Tribunal present there, and it was the lady who said to me, "Oh, another gentleman called Aleksandar is there," and I said, "Well, I don't remember who he was," and then I saw him across the room and he came over and then I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there was not even a suggestion of any blame that you exchanged friendly words with someone you had already even forgotten his name. The issue is: I asked you whether there was any exchange of documents. Your answer was "no" and that was, as it appears now, the wrong answer. Secondly, I instructed you, because that was my second question to you, not to speak with anyone about your testimony. That included the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood your question to mean what I've just explained. Whether I gave the other witness -- I mean, as I said, I might have misunderstood. As to communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I do understand from your last words that you wanted to respond to my question. My question is that you communicated with the Defence team through documents. I instructed you not to speak with anyone about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement was shown on television and everybody saw that, and some even told me about it in a slightly distorted manner. And it was on every TV station, B2 and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I instructed you at the end of your testimony a little bit over one week ago not to speak with anyone about your testimony. Nevertheless, you felt free to give documents to another witness to give that to the Defence team, which means that you initiated communication with the Defence team where you were instructed to refrain from any conversation about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that the request was to submit the documents to someone, and I didn't know how I was supposed to do that, since I was banned from communicating with anyone, and I had to submit the documents that I was asked to submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you submit the documents -- you told me that you received the documents you were requested to bring with you, that you received that request only yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the request last night, and I received the documents last night by fax. And when I faxed here. So it got to the hotel fax. You can tell on the basis of the fax number and the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, isn't it true that apart from a list of those who attended, and apart from the minutes of the Prnjavor meetings, that you gave other documents so that the Defence team could have a look at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I gave him this kind of diploma and acknowledgment in my name that I received for my merits in promoting peace and security in the municipality, and I was the only person in the entire municipality who received that certificate. And I got it in 1994, and I've got the original here with me, and I got it from the Municipal Assembly, mixed Municipal Assembly, and it was for everything I did in the course of the war. And it is the highest possible prize or honour that somebody could get at all. And I don't think anyone else has ever received anything like that. And I felt that it was a good idea to submit it, and this is the photocopy and I've got the original with me. And perhaps I -- yeah, I should explain what it's about. I don't know whether the Defence will understand why I'm submitting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have a talent, Mr. Vasic, a well-developed talent, not to address the matters what it's really about. You gave us ten lines of explanation of a diploma. Did you give any personal opinions on developments in the early 1990s? So not a document, but just your own views on matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything I've said here in the course of the trial, that is to say, that the Muslims left Prnjavor in 1991, in 1990, and in 1995, in the course of exchanges, was all aimed at a practical explanation for the decisions of the UNHCR, OSCE, and OHCE for -- OHR, sorry, with regard to ownership and property, et cetera. And we were the first one which properly implemented those decisions. And just to clarify matters, why were we the first? Because during the war, we were not driving Muslims out of their own homes. It was an economic immigration that happened. And then there were exchanges in 1995. And this is something that I mentioned in my statement, that in 1991, because of family reunions, people took their women and children and about 2.000 Muslims left in that way and then -- and yes, it was all by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was by way of explanation? Any handwritten document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything I've written, I explained -- I mean, this is by way of explanation as to why I received those honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, would you please have a look at this document. Mr. Vasic, is that a document you gave to Mr. Divcic in order to give it to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you write it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document may be returned. The document may be returned, Madam Usher. I suggest to the parties that the document will be marked for identification. The original to be returned to you, Mr. Josse, a copy to be kept in the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Am I allowed to ask questions about it in due course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. A copy will be made during the first break so that you have a copy available. Mr. Vasic, do I understand that -- let me just show you from a distance. You talked about a kind of a diploma. Is that this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is informed that there was some correspondence between the deputy High Representative and Mr. Subotic and Zivkovic. Are these documents you gave to Mr. Divcic in order to give them to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally, there's one document which seems to be correspondence from the organisation for security and cooperation in Europe to Mr. Zivkovic, sent by Igor Licina, OSCE Banja Luka. Is that a document you gave to Mr. Divcic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the document I was just explaining a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you did, Mr. Vasic, is to give further explanations where you were instructed not to speak with anyone, including Defence counsel, further explanations directly related to your testimony. You should have refrained from doing that. The documents will be put in the hands of the registrar. A copy will be made available to the Prosecution. All documents will be marked for identification. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed to address you. Upon arriving here, I received a note instructing me to submit the necessary documents, and I believe that all the documents stated herein were the ones that I was supposed to submit. Some of these documents I was unable to obtain, even the ones that I obtained, I was unable to contact the Defence team, and I was asking for a fax number of the ICTY in order to deliver to them the Merhamet documents containing numbers of the Muslims. As for this particular document, this was a document from the ICTY that I believe that I had to act upon the instructions and deliver the documents somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, did I ask you in the beginning whether you received a request for bringing with you information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you then explain to me what documents you were able to obtain and that others you could not obtain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they might have come through the fax already, but since I am not in contact with the staff there, I'm not aware of that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you what I put to you. I asked you whether you received the request. I asked you whether you were able to obtain, and then you explained to us that, through telefax, you were only able to obtain a list of those who attended the municipality meetings and full minutes. You did not speak about any further explanations, any further personal opinions about the events in the early 1990s. It now turns out that you provided to the Defence team, through Mr. Divcic, your personal opinion about certain matters in a handwritten document, accompanied by some other documents you did not mention before. I hope that that's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not. Your Honour, the first I was told that the Defence gave this to be given to me. I'm not really aware of the rules. I know that I'm not allowed to contact the Defence. But if somebody tells me that I was given this document by the Defence, I read the letter stating under number 2 that I needed to provide full lists of Muslims who left Prnjavor in 1992, 1993, and 1994. And as I was unable to obtain the documents containing the information, I tried to provide the information in writing. The information now in the meantime might have arrived. And I believe that the Defence was aware of the Rules and of the proper way of communicating with me. I was told that it was the Defence that provided this document for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the Chamber has heard enough about it. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let's begin with the destruction of the mosques at Lisnja and Poraci. The one at Lisnja was quite old, a couple of hundred years old; right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw it in my life. I don't know how old it was, but I suppose you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was constructed of thick stone, much in the fashion of the Ferhadpasa mosque in Banja Luka, stone as thick as a metre wide?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that two Muslim soldiers told me and another person that the mosque was on fire and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I have a certain amount of time. I asked you a question. You answered the question. If anyone is interested in a rehash of your previous testimony, they'll ask.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a result of the construction of that mosque, it took explosives to bring it down, isn't that right, and the mosque was blown up with explosives during or shortly after the operation in Lisnja; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the operation in Lisnja and not after the operation. I did not hear an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it was done by the forces you mentioned earlier which participated in the operation in Lisnja, that is, the police and the TO, including the Wolves of Vucjak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and the army, because the Wolves of Vucjak were members of the army, but they were simply popularly called the Wolves of Vucjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to next address the letter that you showed the Court from Merhamet. That was included in tab 10 of the materials you provided. And you stressed, in particular, when you presented that letter, that no representative of the municipal authorities was present at that meeting. First of all, Mr. Vasic, there was a Prnjavor policeman present at that meeting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and I don't think so, although I cannot tell you with any precision. Because I see that this was delivered to the chief of the public security station, so it was sent over to him, which means that he wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how you can derive the conclusion first of all that the chief to whom it was sent wasn't present, and even further, that an emissary, representative of the police was not present, but you raise an interesting point. That letter --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I told you, I don't know exactly. But I don't think that he was present, because it wasn't really customary for the UNHCR to have a meeting and not write a list of attendees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what you do know is that that letter was written with the awareness that Serbian municipal authorities, including the police and including the head of the municipality, would read it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter was sent to us for our information, probably because they wanted also to show us that the municipal authorities did provide a certain degree of protection to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who sent that letter to the municipal authorities? It wasn't UNHCR; right? They don't make a habit of sending their internal correspondence or correspondence reflecting their meetings with victims to municipal authorities, do they?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this through internal mail every day. I received some 10 to 15 documents, including this one. I believe that this document arrived from Merhamet by mail. I know for a fact that I was not handed it personally by someone, but through mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that letter was sent by Merhamet because Prnjavor municipal authorities insisted that any meetings or complaints, any meetings with internationals by non-Serbs in the municipality go through Serbian authorities or that information about such meetings be provided to Serbian authorities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such form of an ultimatum. This wasn't something that I was given to doing, issuing ultimatums or blackmails.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why don't we look at a document that was produced in 1992, where Serbian municipal authorities were not present and where they were not copied on the document. That's P794, which is contained at tab 34. On the third page of that document, there's a special report --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Perhaps it's my problem, but the bundle I've got only goes up to tab 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the new bundle that was distributed this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. morning, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't been given that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I provided it to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been provided to Mr. Stewart. There's an additional copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the third page of that document reflects a special report on minorities in the Prnjavor area, and specifically, a meeting that was held with members of the Ukrainian minority community in Prnjavor on June 13th, 1992. As you'll see in the third paragraph of that report, the document notes that at an earlier meeting with the Czech and Slovak communities, a member of the SDS was present, but at this meeting, no member of the SDS was present. At paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made this point on the last occasion when we were pressed for time. The witness needs to read the whole document. One really cannot cross-examine on a selective way like this, in my submission. I need to read the whole document, and so does the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The whole document is not relevant, Your Honour. I'm directing the witness's attention and counsel's attention to portions of that document. If the witness wants some time after his attention is directed to those portions, of course I understand, but it seems absurd to me to invite the witness to read irrelevant parts of the document rather than focussing his attention on the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness to answer questions on specific portions and give him an opportunity perhaps during the first break, and giving you an opportunity as well, Mr. Josse, to see whether any portion is taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as I have my learned friend's assurance that nothing else in it could possibly affect the answer that he's going to give, then I accept that, but only on that condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you'll have an opportunity to verify that during the first break. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let me direct your attention to paragraph 6 of that special report, which indicates that the members of the minorities have desired to contact members of the EC teams operating in the area, but were told that requests are to go through the municipality offices controlled by the SDS, and indeed in some instances, minority group representatives were threatened not to contact EC teams. That's in fact what was happening at the time, Mr. Vasic, isn't it, and that's why the Merhamet letter too was copied to the municipality authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the letter of Merhamet -- from Merhamet was delivered on the 30th of May, 1995. I don't know who wrote this, but of course the municipal authorities were controlled by the SDS, because the SDS won the majority seats in the elections. That is why. As for these minorities mentioned here, they responded to military call-ups in far greater numbers than the Serbs, and many of them got killed, and they were very loyal to the Serb state, and this isn't -- this simply isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you can deny it if you want, but please refrain from providing a great deal of unrelated testimony about tangential matters raised in this report. I'll put the question to you simply yes or no, that from late 1991 and early 1992, the SDS in Prnjavor and in other parts of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, demanded that minority groups go through the municipality offices controlled by the SDS if they wanted to contact internationals. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that this simply isn't true that we barred them from contacting members of the EC. That is simply not true. The municipal authorities did not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that was not the question. The question was whether any contacts were channelled through the municipal authorities. Mr. Tieger didn't ask you whether you allowed them or whether you barred them, but did they have to go through the municipal authorities to establish these kind of contacts. That was the question, and not any other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not make these contacts through the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have to apply for approval or do they have to apply in whatever way, or did they have to inform the municipal authorities about their wish to seek contact with the internationals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, and I was familiar with these issues, no. Now, as to whether such a requirement existed with the police, I would not know about that, because I was not informed about these matters and it was not within my purview. As for the municipal authorities, I can tell you that this was not case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you brought with you and showed the Court a letter prepared by Merhamet, knowing that it would be reviewed by municipality authorities in order to show that intimidation and pressure on minorities had not taken place. Can we take a look at what the EC team was told on this occasion when there was no member of the SDS present and when the representatives of the minority community obviously believed that the information would stay between them and the EC? And in that respect, I ask you to look at paragraph 4. Paragraph 4 states that a typical pattern of intimidation was being conducted against the ethnic minorities. And it goes on to enumerate the nature of that pattern, beginning with the spreading of fear, then provocations, such as beatings, continued harassment by police or shootings at night around the houses of minorities. And it was those factors that was causing members of the minority communities to flee. Isn't that in fact an accurate account of what was happening in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my earlier testimony, and I do not wish to repeat it, I stated that at any given time, there were 2.000 soldiers shooting around, and this was something that intimidated both the Serbs and the others. They should not have allowed the soldiers to enter the town armed. I do not know whether it was as a result of these events that the minorities fled. I don't know that there were any Ukrainians among the refugees. I cannot speak for the period after the blowing up of the mosque. The fact is that there were Serb refugees who arrived in Prnjavor, in thousands. I did not deny that there were shootings and that the population in general was being intimidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to another document that you produced and that you sought to bring the Court's attention to, and that was the letter from Bishop Komarica, which was located at tab 9, I think the second document of materials in that tab. And in fact, I'm not going to draw your attention to the details of that, but that was in fact a letter to Mr. Vincic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the police, who implemented my agreement reached with Mr. Komarica in Banja Luka, through the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So in that case, you were taking credit for what the police had done. Now, first of all, Mr. Vasic --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given credit for the agreement reached. I simply submitted this document as proof, contrary to what your witness stated, that all the mosques were torn down. I told you that not a single Catholic church was blown up. And this is the document that I would value, rather than the reports written by different intelligence officers, communists, who hated us immensely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll take a look at such an intelligence report shortly. But before that, I want to ask you about your reliance on Bishop Komarica. First of all, you know very well that Bishop Komarica was widely known for his public and courageous denunciation of widespread ethnic cleansing in the Banja Luka area; he's someone who told the world that ethnic cleansing was taking place in the Autonomous Region of Krajina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did, yes. But not for Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, he also complained to you about violence against minorities in Prnjavor, but you did not bring that particular letter, but it's contained now in the materials at tab 19. Let's take a look that at

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this needs an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 19, Your Honours, will be P955.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this is not a letter to Mr. Vincic. This is a letter directly to you, dated the 3rd of August, 1992. I presume you've seen this before.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did receive this letter, and as a result of this letter, I met with Bishop Komarica, and this meeting then resulted in all the other events that I was given credit for later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the letter, Bishop Komarica notes that Catholics in Prnjavor don't cause trouble, that he is appalled by violence against them and against religious facilities that is being carried out in the municipality, and he complains about the lack of interest of the official public organs to resolve the problems, and even notes that the police have threatened a priest for reporting such an event. That's all correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already explained this earlier. I did not say Greek Catholic, but rather Orthodox Ukrainian priest. And I explained how all this violence came about and how people who were responsible for the events in Kulasi were reported to the police. At the time the bishop was writing the letter, he probably wasn't aware of all the steps that we had already undertaken. The bishop stated here that the church in Kulasi was also destroyed, which was not the case. He was obviously misinformed. It was simply that the priest was beaten up, that a TV set and some other appliances were stolen from the church, and then these eight people were prosecuted as the perpetrators of these deeds. And as a result of all these events, a meeting was held with Bishop Komarica and then further measures were taken. All of this came about after this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll compare the dates of Bishop Komarica's initial letter and the dates of the events that you referred to which were provided in other portions of the materials. But it's a fact, isn't it, that Bishop Komarica was someone who had the ear of the international community and that whatever action, if any, you and Mr. Vincic took was in response to the fact that Bishop Komarica was bringing this to the attention of the international organisations, the international media, and the international community, which had an eye on the Banja Luka area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the situation in Prnjavor, but I am not that well-informed about the situation in general around Prnjavor and I do not wish to speak about that. I know that many Croats and Ukrainians even more, were members of the army and were loyal to the Serbs. Many of them got killed in the war. And that is why all the different minorities in Prnjavor should be regarded in a different manner than others, perhaps. I was an official there, but I am not familiar with what was going on around the municipality. That is all hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber would like to address a matter which seems to be rather urgent. Mr. Josse, you told us about what I understood to be visa problems for one of your witnesses. That's a witness for which no protective measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He will not require protective measures. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can talk about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: His name, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica is on what is often called the blacklist of the European Union, which essentially is a kind of a travel ban within the EU. I did understand that the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs expected a safe conduct to be ordered by the Trial Chamber in order to grant a visa to Mr. Bjelica, and if there will be any other witnesses which are on similar lists, the same would be true. I've given it some thought. I have briefly discussed the matter with the Victims and Witnesses Section. I was a bit surprised that a safe conduct would be the solution, because every witness who arrives in Dutch territory enjoys a safe conduct as far as the Dutch government is concerned, under the host agree. That means that safe conducts usually are issued in order to protect witnesses against prosecution by anyone else, third countries or even by the Office of the Prosecution. Because the safe conduct, as far as the Dutch government is concerned, is in the host agreement. Therefore, I think the problem is a different one. The problem being that the Dutch government might be inclined, or let's say it in the negative, might not be inclined not to apply the agreed common position of the EU unless there would be a clear expression by the Tribunal that it would be in the interests of justice to make this witness enter Dutch territory to testify and then to leave the territory again, which would not require a safe conduct, but rather would require the Dutch government to prioritise at that moment the interests of the Tribunal above any travel limitations imposed by the European Union. At the same time, the reasons -- I mean, the purpose of this travel ban, or blacklist, is to impose sanctions on individuals who are engaged in activities which help persons at large continue to evade justice or who are otherwise acting in a manner which could obstruct the ICTY's work. And of course it would be a snake that bites in its own tail to say because of the EU restrictions, you're not allowed to enter the Dutch territory, which would prevent you from testifying before this Tribunal, which of course would not serve the interests of justice, would not serve the interest of the ICTY. So therefore, I suggest to the parties that this Chamber will give a written instruction to the Registrar to address the Dutch government through the minister of foreign affairs, requesting, because we usually address governments by way of requests rather than by any orders, unless there is a clear reason to expect that requests would not be taken seriously , to request the Dutch government not to apply the common position agreed within the EU not to allow one of the persons on the list entrance, but for the limited purposes of testifying before this Court, to apply the host agreement, giving entry to this country, giving safe conduct as far as the Dutch government is concerned, and to apply whatever other limitations the Dutch government might feel necessary. I suggest that the Chamber would give such an instruction to the Registry, as a matter of urgency. I do understand that I can imagine that the Registry would first consult with the Dutch government to see whether what kind of wording one might need, but in order to resolve this matter as soon as possible, I think the first step would be that in such an instruction, this Chamber expresses as its view that it's important that it's in the interest of justice that the Defence can call the witnesses it wants to call, in the interest of the defence of Mr. Krajisnik. Any submission in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. We had begun making some inquiries. We were clearly barking to some extent up the wrong tree. We were approaching the matter in the wrong way. The request to the Registry by the Chamber will, no doubt, assist matters. There's still a minor logistical problem. For example, Mr. Bjelica lives in Sokolac. He's almost certainly going to have to travel to Belgrade, because I was told there will be a problem with him coming via a third country, in other words, another EU country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be a third country, then of course the safety conduct under the host agreement would not apply and then we would have to issue a safe conduct for any transit country. Under those circumstances, we would need a safe conduct because the safe conduct in the host agreement is of course limited to the Dutch authorities and does not apply to German, Belgian, whatever other authorities. But I was informed from Belgrade a direct flight would be possible, which would result in no need for any safe conduct in respect of third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If there's any difficulty with that, then I would refer to either the Court or the Registry. I should say that originally, Mr. Bjelica had been lined up for the end of this week. When these problems became apparent, he was called off, so to speak. In fact, that may not be such a bad thing, because he did provide me, on my recent trip to Bosnia, with a significant number of documents. They're being sorted out before being submitted to the CLSS. And therefore, so far as he is concerned, there is no immediate urgency, but I am very grateful to Your Honour and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If in any future situation you would have -- if you would face this kind of difficulties which are, to a large extent, of a legal nature, in which you would need the help of the Chamber, do not hesitate to ask for it. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no submissions as to the solution proposed by the Trial Chamber. Our only request is that we are aware that Mr. Bjelica provided a significant number of documents and it's our request that at some point in time before he testifies in 14 days before he testifies that we receive the translations of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, perhaps you could already inform Mr. Bjelica that if he thinks that he has relevant and important documents available to him at this moment, that if he doesn't provide them to you at shortish notice, that there might be a risk that there would be no opportunity to look at them. And I take it that relevance would primarily be relevance for the Defence, of course for the truth, but we know that looking at the truth from different points of view could influence the selection of documents you would find most relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, to be fair to him, he gave me a large number of documents. In fact, the gentleman to my left, who I was about to introduce, Mr. Marko Sladojevic, who has recently joined our team, has been tasked by me with looking through those documents. He in fact did me a preliminary report last night and that's a matter I'm going to discuss with him later today. But this witness will not be called in the immediate future, for these two reasons that the Chamber has identified, partly the documents, partly his travel arrangements. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then I take it that you filled in -- well, we heard from Mr. Stewart about the remainder of this week. We'll discuss the matter this afternoon, how to deal with these intervals. Let me be quite clear that of course the Chamber is finally not going to accept the situation in which we say, well, we have got one witness for this week and then perhaps another one for the next week. I mean, that certainly will not be accepted by the Chamber. But we'll further discuss the matter. May I take it that if you have postponed the testimony of Mr. Bjelica, that you're doing your utmost best to get other witnesses in time here, so as to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I devote a lot of my time to this particular problem. I'm hoping there are going to be two shortish witnesses here for the four-day week next week. That's the present plan. Perhaps I could report back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. An application form was with the VWS, so I was told by Mr. Karganovic, at 9.00 this morning for those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, you may be aware that even although we had a recess and even although I was not in this country, that I was kept informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- minute for minute on when you had delays for your flights, well, whatever you did, and you informed us. So therefore, don't be afraid that it has not the full attention of this Chamber. Then any other matter in relation to this? If similar situations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would arise in respect of other witnesses appearing on similar lists, please take the necessary measures well in time. I'll inform you tomorrow where we stand on the matter of safe conduct or the whole Mr. Bjelica. In that respect, I'd like to get a scheduling -- well, scheduling information from the Defence, because even if it's no safe conduct, you'll understand that making an exception to the blacklist would be limited in time, and therefore we would have to know exactly when you expect Mr. Bjelica to arrive to testify or to be prepared for his testimony, so that we could introduce that in the conversations between the Dutch government and the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour wants that done in open court, could I deal with that tomorrow? Otherwise, administratively, within the next 24 hours, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could do it by tomorrow morning, that would be fine. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, two matters, one extremely brief. Through an oversight, we didn't have those additional documents from the Prosecution tabs until the break, but we have got them now, both Mr. Krajisnik and I. Secondly, and rather more importantly, it's this: The reason Mr. Karganovic is not in Court is I've caused him to make some inquiries about what passed between Messrs. Divcic and Vasic. I do want a full answer in relation to that before I have a chance to re-examine Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me turn into private session for one minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To bring Mr. Vasic into the courtroom again and then he may continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, please be seated. Mr. Tieger will continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just ask a question before we go on? Since in the beginning I was very shaken by this misunderstanding that we discussed, maybe it was my fault, but there's this letter which is of key importance with reference to all the events that was not included in that set of documents. I would like you to take account of that letter. Because ten days ago, our lawyer said that he would be in touch with me through the Tribunal's services, but he hasn't been in touch with me. And the arrival of the official from the Tribunal and the handing over of this letter was something that I considered a contact, a form of contact. However, I don't know whether it was done on purpose or not. Everything was written in English and I don't understand English. There are only two sentences in a language that I understand, and there was a request for documents and I tried to submit all the documents. I submitted one and I didn't submit the other, and I tried to explain this. And I was not given any instructions as to how to submit this sort of document, so I tried to make do. And the first person that I set eyes on that I knew was going to meet them, I thought it would have been permitted. And so that's why I acted the way I did. And it was not my intention to establish contacts for any other reason. And I would also like you to take account of this letter because that led to this confusion on my part, more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the letter by the Victims and Witnesses Section in which you are invited to bring documents with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to get him to hand it in as part of my re-examination. Why doesn't Your Honour look at it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to suggest Your Honour looks at it now or it can wait until re-examination. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at what letter the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court official did say to me that this came from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will return it to the witness. We received, as a matter of fact, a copy of it. I do understand that this is the translation by the Victims and Witnesses Section, not literally translation, but the transfer of a request by one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In Mr. Vasic's absence in due course, I will give a full history of the matter. I'm quite anxious to see what's written on the envelope, because that may have some bearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Yes. I have not looked at the envelope. I just have looked at the ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says "for your information." "Please ask Mr. Vasic to bring the documents as described in this letter on Tuesday to the Tribunal." I was informed that the Victims and Witnesses Section received the request only last Friday and that therefore it was of no use to try to send it to the former Yugoslavia, but rather to wait until he would arrive and then give it to him personally. And then there's an indication of the hotel where to find Mr. Vasic which I'll not read out in open court. Then, Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, before we adjourned, you had explained that at the time the bishop wrote the letter, the first letter we've been referring to, he wasn't -- he probably wasn't aware of all the steps that you had already undertaken and was misinformed about what happened in the church in Kulasi because what happened, according to you, was simply that the priest was beaten up, that a TV set and some other appliances were stolen, and that eight people were prosecuted. That latter information about eight people was something you talked about in your earlier testimony; is that right? That's an incident you referred to earlier and brought to the Court's attention in the materials you provided?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that the case was processed. I knew -- I mean, I mentioned that I had a meeting with the citizens in the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You pointed out a document referring to the church in Kulasi and eight alleged perpetrators, I think, on your second day of testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yeah. I can't remember correctly, but yes, I must have done, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can explain, then, how Bishop Komarica could have been misinformed about this incident in which the priest was abused, a TV set stolen, and eight individuals allegedly involved, when that incident did not take place until more than three months after the bishop's letter. The incident in Kulasi, to which you referred and which was the subject of your earlier testimony, occurred on the 27th of November, 1992, according to the documents that you provided; isn't that right? And let me refer the Court and counsel's attention to the LiveNote of October 11th, at page 12.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Komarica was probably misinformed, and I was actually referring to the fact that, amongst other things -- I mean, and he did indicate that there were two facts, that there were shooting and people were frightened and all that, but he also indicated that the church was destroyed in the paper that you showed me earlier. And it wasn't fully destroyed, and so that's what I was referring to when I said he must have been misinformed. And I mean now everything that's being indicated by Bishop Komarica was taking place in relation to everyone, without distinction. I've said it a hundred times already. The fact that people were frightened by shooting and that they were being intimidated. It is just a part of my story that I'm not going to repeat for the umpteenth time here. But it is a fact that all attempts were being made in order to normalise things. I had already mentioned before that we made an official request for General Talic to ban soldiers from carrying weapons and I had a meeting with the [indiscernible] at the factory and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you're repeating your earlier testimony. It's not in response to any question I asked.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Bishop Komarica was referring not to the incident you drew our attention to earlier, not to the incident in which there was a criminal report against eight perpetrators in late November for beating up the priest and ransacking the church, but to an earlier incident of a similar sort?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood the letter by Bishop Komarica, it was a general statement about pressures, events, et cetera, and a specific reference to the church having been destroyed. But I don't know about that. I know that the church at Kulasi had not been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. The fact is that Bishop Komarica referred to an incident, and then you tried to tell us, oh, that incident had been taken care of and eight perpetrators had been arrested, when in fact that incident upon which you relied didn't take place until three months later, and in fact the documents you provided don't even indicate they were arrested, just that a criminal report was filed. In short, Bishop Komarica was referring to an incident about which there was no action, and you tried to convince us it was an incident about -- over which action had been taken; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not just one event, actually. There are dozens of events. Amongst other things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let me be -- try to listen to the questions. Mr. Tieger asked you the following: In one of your earlier responses, you said a response was given to the event described by the bishop because against eight persons action was taken, or at least reports filed, whatever. That's what you said in response to that question. Now Mr. Tieger confronts you with the fact that you earlier testified about action taken on the basis of an event which took place on the 27th of November. And therefore, he says, the events described in this first letter a couple of months before, I do not understand how you can tell us that action -- or that a response was given to that letter, where you told us before that this response or this action was taken as a response to something that happened on the 27th of November and not somewhere in July or August. That's the question. Therefore, clearly explain to us whether any specific action against eight individuals was taken as a result of this letter or whether it is your testimony that only eight individuals were taken action against, reports, whatever way, as a result of something that happened in November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain that similar events took place before and afterwards. And matters had always been undertaken. Obviously 12 or 13 years later I can't be quite sure which of those events happened three months later or three months before. But, for example, this Ukrainian church that is being referred to as Greek Catholic church, I said that when there was an attempt to destroy the Roman Catholic Church, the perpetrators were arrested and one woman recognised one of them, but they were military personnel and so they were handed over to the military authorities, and one of them was from Banja Luka and one of them was from Cilinesa [phoen]. We didn't just take all the necessary measures in order to be able to solve this problem. And we did undertake many other measures as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the speaker slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the event at Kulasi was not to do with this letter. I simply made a reference that within the overall context of all these events. Because, Your Honour, there was a persistent effort in trying to prove that religious -- places of religious worship were being destroyed and people were being frightened, and I'm trying to prove that this is not the case. And as to how many events there were and how many measures were taken, well, this is 12 or 13 years ago, so I don't know. I'm trying to prove that the authorities did their job properly within limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you be very precise. The action taken against, as you said, these eight people were prosecuted as the perpetrators of those deeds, did that happen after the 27th of November events or did that happen at any time earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I may fall into the trap of giving the wrong date, but if there is an event with reference to a Greek Catholic Church, measures were taken prior to this letter. And the event of the destruction of the Roman Catholic Church, in case it was earlier. But what I'm trying to say is that the police forces tried to keep things under control at all times. Perhaps I should check the dates in my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you testified about eight people being prosecuted as the perpetrators of these deeds. What deeds did you have in mind? Anything that happened in November or anything that happened in - what was it? - July, August? August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those eight people were arrested due to the events that took place in relation to the Kulasi and Kopa Lozancic church. It must have been in November, obviously, as the Prosecution is claiming, but this was just one in a series of events and one in a series of measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I want to move now to a telephone conversation, an intercepted telephone conversation, involving three persons. We have two clips for that. The transcript of that conversation is contained at tab 3. And I believe it needs a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be, Your Honours, P956.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let me say at the outset that I'm not going to play the entire intercept in the interests of time. I'll play two portions of it. The entire transcript is available to you, however, if -- should it become necessary in the course of responding to any question. If we could begin, then, with the first clip. I have a couple of brief questions for you about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate for the interpreters and for the Court what page, what box?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That should begin on the first page, Your Honour, and consume basically the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What's up, Dragan? There's nothing. The army was called up, mobilisation, TO, and in local communities, take away and so on. I see. And who mobilised the TO? TO district staff did. District staff? Yes, district staff. There's an order. Order from whom? Just a moment. Who issued the order? It is from the command in Banja Luka. From the command in Banja Luka. Yes. Okay, Dragan. I mean, nothing has been done without an order. No, no, I just wanted to know if it was from Sarajevo or Banja Luka. From Banja Luka, from Banja Luka. From Banja Luka, excellent. You know what? We have -- I have a small problem. I think it is a bigger one. Yes. That's why I insisted to talk to you. The first one is this thing with Cvijic, it was carried out. The thing regarding civilian protection, but not everything. However, it doesn't matter. But the second thing, he did not observe our agreement. He took the stamp and he carries it around. I see. We don't have a stamp. We don't know what to do. I will send you a letter, decision of the party board, which has been unanimously adopted. So if you could order him or maybe I could call you, if you have some time to come to one of our meetings. Fucking hell. I should come. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know the French translation sometimes is a little slower. I'm just waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to ask Judge Hanoteau to inform us. Judge Hanoteau was following the English. But I take it that this now took so much time, I'll change to French. This now took so much time that the French translation will have finished. Otherwise, I'll hear from anyone. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the record, this is telephone conversation dated 25 September 1991. Mr. Vasic, did you recognise the two persons speaking, the voices of the two persons speaking?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the president of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it then was, Radovan Karadzic, and the MP from Prnjavor, Dragan Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- turn your attention next to the second clip of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters, that begins --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. There seems to be a mistake here. It says Cvijic, but it's Vidic, the president of the party, Dobrivoje Vidic, in relation to this stamp. I don't know what kind of disagreement there must have been between the two of them and one of them got the stamp. I don't know what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I was just about to mention that the second clip begins at page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Dragan, and take care of things, for fuck's sake. He's the municipality president. Okay. Doctor, how are you? Thank God, I'm fine. I'm Nemanja, president here. I have seen you here a couple of times. Twice you were here. I'm glad to talk to you. I remember. We usually communicate through Dragan and the guy with the beard. Yes, yes, president of the Executive Committee, Radivojevic. I see. Please, take care of Dobrivoje, pay him some respect but ... well, it's getting a bit better. I mean, it is a bit difficult to deal with him, you know. I know, I know, what he's like. To avoid explaining ... I know what he's like. And regarding the biggest problems on arms, that is settled. I know what he is like. That is settled. But in general I have control of the situation in the municipality in full and I can tell you that we are one of the rare municipalities where 111 soldiers were called up and 111 went. Excellent, excellent. Even the Croats and the Muslims went. We had such activity and it worked. I see. And people responded well to training. Good. Through them. I called the Muslim officers from the staff and I told them: If you were honest when you put on the uniforms, then go to these villages and tell people to respond to the calls, if you did not ... so they left and it all worked. Excellent, fine. Everything, apart from this thing with the SUP, this is difficult, doesn't work. Did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you reach the agreement with the Muslims that the commander is yours? Yes.
