We sent it up to MUP in writing. All parties and SDA and us in Prnjavor. Yes. Agree that the commander is a Serb and the deputy is a Muslim, and if it hasn't been so far until now. And they only did not agree. They called a few times. He won't. He played some games. Vito was here and promised in two days. They're playing games. They probably want the Muslim commander, that's it. Yes, they said it openly. But until now commander, deputy and secretary were all Serbs and it didn't bother them. But now they're pushing it to be that way. People are prepared and the Assembly adopted a decision and now just because of that it turns out that this government is not capable. How many Muslims are there in total? In percentages, there are four to five per cent, and the chief of the crime service is a Muslim. I see. The SUP deputy will be the Muslim, deputy commander. So, practically, they'll have 23 per cent. Only 14 per cent of them. And they have 23 per cent of power there. They'll have 23 per cent of power. Okay. Yes. They have 18 per cent in reserve formations and there are 14 per cent of them in the municipality. I mean, we have them a bit more everywhere so they cannot complain. I see. But it doesn't work. This change is not happening. It seems that it is in their interest to ... Okay. I will call Zepinic now to try to push even though according to some agreement ... so, how many of them are there in the municipality, 14 per cent? 14 per cent something. And how much power they got, the parties? The parties, they got 9.8 per cent. 9.8? Yes. Well, this is below 10 per cent. They cannot get commander. You're right. They cannot get commander below. Well, they are the fourth party in the municipality. The party is the second, reformists third, they're fourth. Okay, but from ruling ones ... they're not ruling. Yes, yes. The others are not ruling. Yes. I will now call Zepinic in Odzak. Okay, so ... all the best. Okay, thank you. And appoint that man. Let me be there. Introduce him and they may accept him one day. We cannot. And how, when the secretary is not allowed, cannot, you know. My god, you Serbs just stick to the law. How come it cannot? Stojan Zupljanin from Banja Luka will. He is the head of the regional office. Yes. If we wanted to appoint him, we would pay for it. It wouldn't be a problem. Make an agreement with him and if the MUP does not want to accept it, you just appoint him. Then I will say that you told Stojan, that you gave a green light that he does it. Just appoint him and let them go to fucking hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, if you could quickly identify the participants in that latter part of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part is President Karadzic and I myself, as the president of the municipality. This was my first conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have one question for you. Shortly after your conversation with Dr. Karadzic begins and after there's a brief discussion about Radivojevic and taking care of Dobrivoje, you advise Dr. Karadzic that regarding the biggest problem on arms, that is settled. What was that problem, Mr. Vasic, and how did you settle it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arms, the TO arms, were distributed according to the orders from Banja Luka. The arms were to be distributed and the then operator in Prnjavor, somebody called Debeljak, who was afraid of it and he sent a letter saying that he did not dare to do that, even though it was in line with the TO law. And then afterwards we followed this from Banja Luka and it was the district staff that was bound, duty-bound, to do that, and so we carried out the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, it was the case, was it not, that in fact weapons were being smuggled into Prnjavor by Serbian officials, including yourself, for the purpose, as you viewed it, of defending the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never in my life did I smuggle weapons. I was the president, and I was in charge of the municipality as such. I claim with full responsibility that the municipal staff never smuggled any weapons. There may have been such incidents that were then dealt with by the police. There may have been such incidents, but they were definitely not carried out in an organised manner or under the auspices of the authorities, but rather than individuals trying to procure weapons for themselves for their own protection, which was of course contrary to the law. Mr. Prosecutor, we were discussing about the numbers of the Muslims armed, numbers of those who responded to the TO call-ups. These were recruits who formed the regular forces. I wasn't referring to the persons in general but to the recruits who were sent into the army. This conversation must be dated before the war, although I don't have the date before me, because before the war it was through the army and the recruitment centre that people were recruited, both the Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. And then it was only at a later stage that Croats refused to respond to the call-ups, Muslims responded to a certain extent, and of course the Serbs responded 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm not suggesting that there was not any discussion about mobilisation but that there was also a discussion about arming. And in that connection, I would ask you to turn to a document located at tab 8, which is a report prepared by an intelligence officer. I think you referred earlier to reports written by different intelligence officers, and I told you we'd have an opportunity to look at one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It needs a new exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 8 will be given Prosecution P957 and the English translation will be 957.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this document is entitled summary of information of interest for security in Prnjavor municipality. And as you can see, it begins with a great deal of detailed information about the demographics and background of Prnjavor and then goes on to an evaluation of the political parties, the executive government, the administrative organs, the public security station, and is dated 15 March 1992. First of all, Mr. Vasic, is this the kind of intelligence report that you were referring to when you indicated that you would prefer or that you would credit the reports that you had brought to court rather than reports written by different intelligence officers who, as you put it, "hated us immensely"?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents I brought here were the ones that bore the stamp of an institution and the signature of the person who drafted the document, and I'm prepared to defend any such document. As for the documents originating from intelligence officers who do not place any stamps on them and sign themselves in code-names, they contained merely subjective views of the persons drafting these documents and these were persons who hated us immensely because we came to power after 50 years of Communist rule. They, as remnants of the Communist system, remained in the ranks of intelligence organs. And I have to tell you that we had more conflicts with these cadres from the former system than with the so-called nationalist parties. We even entered into a coalition with the SDA. These were reports by persons who followed the political events in all these municipalities that after 1990 had a multi-party system. I proved myself, I believe, to be quite a knowledgeable person about these events rather than the person who wrote this report, who is a good for nothing and who signed himself in a code-name. An illustration of the worthlessness of these documents is the one that originated from the General Staff, where you have the corps commander signing orders for these same units and calling them the 1st Assault Battalion, whereas in a different document they are described as paramilitary units. These were persons working for the intelligence service in the Communist system. And in every single municipality you had about a hundred such people who were tasked with shadowing people, monitoring what these people were doing, down to what they were eating. And I believe that their reports do not even deserve to be commented upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you've made your position clear about these intelligence officers who were shadowing people. Let's just focus for one moment, and I'll give you a chance to either accept or deny the points raised by this operative. Number 1: The operative states that extremist tendencies predominate in the senior leadership of the party. It states that in the very second paragraph. Is that accurate or not? It's the first sentence of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here that they have a tendency to divide. Well, of course every person has a tendency to lean either towards a more moderate or a more extremist position. Perhaps Djuric was considered a more extremist nationalist and I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, your attention is drawn to the previous line, which reads: "But extremist tendencies predominate in the senior leadership of this party." It's not the first time that you are drawing our attention to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Predominate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the first time that you are drawing our attention to something which is not included in the question. I would not prevent you from telling us any relevant matters, but please first respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated in my reply that not all of us are the same, but none of us were really extremists, because if there were such people, then we would have had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the leadership of the SDS in Prnjavor, as indicated in the first sentence of the second paragraph under the heading "evaluation by political parties" espouse a struggle against the Muslims? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hold a leadership position in the SDS, but there were two such leaders, president, who was Dobrivoje Vidic at the time, and a vice-president. Dobrivoje Vidic was considered to be a more moderate person, whereas Dragan Djuric was considered to hold harsher views. However, the leadership, as such, was regarded as moderate, although not even Djuric could be regarded an extremist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just one more section. If you look at -- just one more question. If you look at the section marked "executive government." The second sentence of the second paragraph, or first full paragraph, states: "The president of the Assembly is Nemanja Vasic, an economist, director of Autoprevoz, professionally competent, but as yet politically inexperienced, inclined towards the extreme faction, involved in the smuggling of arms, oil, and other things." Now, first of all, I think it's difficult to tell from that. It may be difficult to tell from that sentence whether the writer is saying that you are inclined toward the extreme faction which is involved in the smuggling of arms, oil, and other things, or whether you yourself are involved in the smuggling of arms, oil, and other things. But with both of those possibilities in mind, can you tell us whether you regard that statement as accurate -- that sentence, rather, as accurate.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are a small municipality, and the people would not have given me 90 per cent or so of their votes if I had been involved in such dealings. These are unmitigating lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, you're aware that there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, sir, that this report had been drawn up by somebody who was biased, hostile to you, et cetera. Do you know who was the recipient of this report? This report, who was it drafted for? Who was it addressed to? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two intelligence services, perhaps even more. There was the military and the police intelligence service. This person, as many others within the Communist system, worked for one of these; I don't know which. But they differ in very insignificant details in their views of the political parties that came to life after the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you did not answer my question. Who was this report for, and who had it been drafted for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. They all had their superiors in the intelligence service hierarchy, but I'm not aware of that and it's very strange. I was never involved in such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as president of this municipality, did you have any knowledge of such reports having been drafted by these officials, these men? And did you know who they were addressed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not know the people either. They were always working under cover. It's difficult for you to understand, because you did not live in such a system. These people are among us, but nobody knows who they are. They are writing reports for someone, somewhere. It's all a mystery, really. But they were really powerful under that system. They had some privileges, those who worked in the municipalities. But those who were uncovered were then thrown out of service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, I myself, on a personal level, would really be interested to know who the recipients of these reports were, if it is at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was recovered from the archives of the CSB Banja Luka, that is, the regional police centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was drafted for this regional public security centre in Banja Luka, and it was meant for the higher echelons of power or was it the end of the road for the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The information I just provided the Court is as much as I can say about the route of this particular document. Whether or not a copy of this document was sent further, I'm not in a position to say. However, I think it does clearly shed light on the witness's indication that it was one of the two services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I want to turn next to the suggestion you made in your earlier testimony that the Prnjavor Crisis Staff was isolated from the Republic leadership, and I think your words were "left to its own devices" because there was no corridor.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication flow was very scarce, and we were almost left to our own devices. We did have some communication with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the Republic leadership, it's accurate to say, I think, that the establishment or liberation, or whatever term one would want to use, of the corridor had not yet taken place in May of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates marking the closure of the corridor are known. I'm afraid I might make a mistake by naming a date. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question in this way, then. When virtually the entire Republic leadership visited Banja Luka for the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, 1992, had the corridor been established?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at this time when the corridor was closed down. But this is a matter of common knowledge. I don't wish to go through my papers now. I can't remember. But I do remember that for quite a long period of time, some two months or maybe more, the corridor was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that you do not dispute that - and I'll give you a few examples - Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Stanisic were all present for Police Day in Banja Luka, for a big parade on May 13th, or that there were plans for Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, and Subotic to visit the ARK, as reflected in the ARK Crisis Staff minutes of May 18th, or, as is reflected in a number of Glas articles which are contained in the materials distributed today, that Bogdan Subotic was in the ARK on June 1st, Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic were there on June 2nd, that General Gvero of the Main Staff was there on 7 June. You don't dispute any of those visits, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember, but I don't dispute that. At that time, one could perhaps fly by helicopter and expose their life to risk. But I don't dispute that, and I'm sure it must be documented in the press. I personally don't know. They could have used Red Cross helicopters or other devices. Anyway, I don't know which method of transport they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Glas article, which reflects a visit of Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic on June 2nd, indicates that they were meeting with leading personalities from the politics and security department of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Banja Luka. You don't dispute that either, do you, that that was at least one of the purposes of their visit?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of Prnjavor municipality. It would be quite logical that if they visited Banja Luka, they would go to visit the president of the municipality. They would do the same had they come to Prnjavor. They would come to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then let's focus for a moment on the relationship between the Prnjavor Crisis Staff and the Prnjavor authorities and the ARK Crisis Staff. It's correct to say, is it not, that the ARK Crisis Staff enacted decisions, made decisions which were then followed up on or enacted by the Prnjavor Crisis Staff? And if it's any assistance to you, let me make sure you're provided with both a copy of the ARK Gazette and the Prnjavor Gazette, reflecting various decisions by both bodies. And those are contained in tabs 32 and 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think tab 33, Your Honour, needs a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 33, Your Honour, will be P958, and the English translation will be P958.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasic, it may or may not be necessary for you to look at particular decisions, but I will identify the number as it appears in the relevant gazette so they can be easily located. I indicated I'd give you a few examples of the Prnjavor Crisis Staff acting upon ARK Crisis Staff decisions. First of all, on May 15th, a decision we discussed before, the decision on confiscation of hunting weapons was made "pursuant to item 5 of the decision of the government of AR Krajina." That's contained in item 38 of the Prnjavor Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you guide us to the right page, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the English translation, that's found on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Vasic, if you look to item number 43, the decision of 23 June 1992, on resident searches and confiscation of property, that was taken "on the basis of conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina of 10 June." And that's found at page 10 of the English, Your Honours and counsel. I'll just give you two quick additional examples. Number 44 is a 23 June 1992 decision on movable and immovable property, providing that those who left the territory and failed to report by a certain date will have their property declared the property of the state "in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." That's found at pages 11 and 12 of the English. And finally, number 46 in the Prnjavor Gazette, the decision of 26 June 1992 on mandatory termination of employment for certain categories of employees. And it provides the specifics for that, the number of years of service, the age of the employee. And it precisely tracks the 8 June 1992 decision by the ARK Crisis Staff, which is number 29, and the Prnjavor decision can be found at page 13 of the English. Mr. Vasic, those are all examples of the Prnjavor Crisis Staff acting upon the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff or government; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this period, when the communication with the government of Republika Srpska was severed, we decided to turn to the ARK decisions because they were -- some of them were actually passed as a result of government decisions. And that is how we passed these decisions, and I still stand by these decisions today as I did at the time. I believe that they were proper decisions. We were trying to solve vital problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The last decision we looked at was a decision on termination of employment. That wasn't the only employment-related decision the ARK made. Let me point you and the Court and counsel to a few others. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. First, number 7 of the decisions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina found in the ARK Gazette, made on 11 May 1992, stating that management posts in Krajina enterprises must be filled by persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in the interests of time, let me move directly to the last decision in sequence that I wanted to bring your attention to. That is 22 June 1992 of the ARK conclusions. That's a previous exhibit, P358, which states that: "All executive posts involving a likely flow of information and so on may only be held by the personnel of Serbian nationality." In addition, the decision provides: "These posts may not be held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed by plebiscite or who in their minds have not made it ideologically clear that the SDS is the sole representative of the Serbian people." And for everyone's benefit, that is located in tab 15. Now, in that regard, Mr. Vasic, I want to bring your attention to some of the things in the Prnjavor Gazette and to just a handful of those. So if you're looking at the Prnjavor Gazette, decision number 81, we see the termination of Jervo Jugo [phoen], who was the former director of the agricultural cooperative. At 84, Ejub Didic [phoen], director of the commercial department of the agricultural cooperative. 96, Dzevad Klokic [phoen]. 97, Slavko Kolunic [phoen]. 99, Suad Klokic [phoen]. 106, Nevenko Kuzmanovic [phoen]. And there are others contained in the Prnjavor Gazette. Mr. Vasic, those were all people who were either not of Serbian nationality or who were not considered loyal or who had not made it ideologically clear that the SDS was the sole representative of the Serbian people; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were managers in Prnjavor who were Croats and Ukrainians. These decisions on the removal from certain posts are due to a change in the rules. All the managers were relieved of their duties, and I myself should be among them as the manager of the company where I was, because they were supposed to be given new decisions appointing them under a new title, wartime managers. However, in this process, some managers left, either because they wanted or because they were incapable, like the manager of Sloga and some other managers who were actually not necessarily non-Serbs. For instance, Momcilo Mandic, Slobodan Vukovic, all these are Serbs, and therefore all the managers of companies in Prnjavor who were being relieved and then reappointed but not as managers of companies but as I believe wartime managers or perhaps some other title was given to them. Such were the rules. Oh, it states here, "managers in time of war." So these were merely decisions relieving them from their duties in order for them to be reappointed under a different title. However, the ARK Krajina organs took some decisions that were not really -- did not really make any sense, so we decided to only act upon some of them that we thought were proper. But I myself was not an official of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two questions. Number 1: Are you suggesting that the people I mentioned to you, as well as others contained in the Prnjavor Gazette, were appointed after their termination?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some of them were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And second question --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I may explain, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We won the elections. It was quite a normal procedure, at least in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that those parties that come to power appoint their own people, and this is the case today. We should look at it rationally. You saw the correspondence between the police and in the conversation with Karadzic, that we were discussing the different percentages, and we were trying to reach some agreements. Unfortunately, at that time it was the political aspect that carried greater weight than one's capacity to do the job. And this was normal at the time. But I mentioned three companies where the managers were reappointed, although they were not Serbs. Perhaps there are other such instances of smaller companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask a few questions, Mr. Tieger? You're referring to what happened as a result of elections. What elections did you have in mind specifically to this, well, large number of decisions end of May 1992/early June 1992? What elections did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was saying was that in 1990, November 1990, we came to power after the elections, and these managers were moved around or replaced due to imminent threat of war. So new terminology was coming in, and bodies belonging to political parties tried to come up with some new concept. What I meant were the elections in November 1990 when we came to power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you saying these decisions just after the ARK decision on who could stay in their positions, yes or no, was a result of you winning the 1990 elections? Because that's what you, as I understood it, suggested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain this. In 1990, we won the elections, and with the SDA, we formed a government. And we left the Muslim managers in place who enjoyed the support of the SDA. They continued to act as managers and directors. When, in the month of May, the SDA left the coalition government, and these changes in managerial positions took place, the new municipal majority asked for new ones to be appointed, and the ones that enjoyed the support of the SDA were not left in their jobs and they had left the coalition at some point in May, even though two members of the Executive Committee remained within that body all the way until August. They did not obey the orders coming from their party, or rather, the requests from the party or instructions or whatever. And the members of the Assembly remained until the very end, but they left the executive power. It just happened to coincide in terms of time, but so it turned out that everybody who enjoyed the support of the SDA was replaced at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So late May and early June, as far as timing is concerned, was just a matter of coincidence; do I understand this to be your answer? Had nothing to do with the decision --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it coincided. The ARK decision has nothing to do with it in Prnjavor. These two things coincided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few matters left. I note the time too. I would use that time to try to pare it down as much as possible, so it might be the right time to break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like a few moments before the break with the Court without the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll invite Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. Vasic, we'll resume in approximately half an hour and then finish soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be my relative inexperience, and I appreciate that this may be a rather large topic, and if it is, then I'm not inviting the Chamber to embark on it at the moment. But I too was interested, to put it mildly, in the document introduced at tab 8. And what I need to know, if at all possible, with respect from Your Honours, prior to my re-examining the witnesses, is what the evidential status is of this document. Now, I note that the Prosecution didn't adduce it as part of their own case. They adduced it in cross-examination of the witness. The cross-examination was quite proper inasmuch as my learned friend was inviting Mr. Vasic to accept or deny certain passages. Not surprisingly, Mr. Vasic denied the passages, didn't accept them. It's fairly inevitable, I'd have thought. It's a comment on my part and it's neither here nor there. What I want to know is now that this document has been introduced, whether it has any evidential status over and above the witness's denial of the parts that were put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should first give an opportunity to Mr. Tieger to explain what, in his view, at this moment the evidential status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly understand the point raised by counsel coming from a system that at least at one time was mindful of the manner in which such documents were brought to the attention of the court. I think this document must be regarded in the same light as other documents and subjected to essentially the same kinds of tests, that is, balanced against and weighed against all the other information available in the case, so that the Court can consider it and give it whatever weight it feels it's entitled to receive. So it doesn't have a unique status by virtue of the way it was brought to the attention of the Court. Clearly -- I don't need to belabour this. Obviously there are some documents that have great weight in light of their provenance, the nature of the testimony, and so on. There are other documents that have less. And where this document falls in the spectrum is up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could give you some guidance. Mr. Josse, usually, and that's the practice before this Chamber, we do not take a decision, as you may have noticed, immediately on whether or not a document will be admitted. If there are any -- admitted into evidence, which does not say any more that we can consider it in making the determinations we have to make. If there's any issue of authenticity, we'd like to hear that right away. So if it's on the admission you'd say this is a forgery or this is -- we have got no idea who Clara is, might be the sister of the composer Schumann, then we'd like to hear that immediately. Otherwise we usually decide on the bulk of the documents at the very end. Now let's just assume that -- which is of course not perfectly clear with this document, let's just assume that there's no authenticity issue to be raised in this respect. Then, and let's just take one example about whether Mr. Vasic was involved in smuggling or not. Well, it's quite clear that we have a document in front of us, let's just assume for argument's sake that it is a document which ended up in the archives of an intelligence service of the Banja Luka police, in which it is stated that Mr. Vasic either was involved in smuggling or was associated with others who were associated with smuggling. That's one. Second, we have the testimony of Mr. Vasic, who says that relying on logic, that he could never have been elected if this would be true, which of course immediately raised in my mind whether everyone voting would have known about it. So the logic is, well, to say the least not for the full hundred per cent compelling. So, therefore, if we would have to establish whether Mr. Vasic would be involved in smuggling, I hardly would expect, and let me -- that the Chamber, on the basis of this material, would ever come to such a conclusion. At the same time, if -- of course we do not know, if we get other reports about smuggling or if we get other evidence, it might support that evidence, despite the logic of Mr. Vasic. But you'll understand that a document which is not clear as to its sources, of which we have now heard the testimony of Mr. Vasic that those who were important in the former system were hostile against many people in the new system, that before even accepting it as support of Mr. Vasic's behaviour, that we would be very cautious, or even reluctant, to do that. I hope that I explained sufficiently that the document, as such, could play a role, although not sufficient in itself to establish any firm fact, in, well, understanding some of the events and the power structures in the municipality. But you don't have to be afraid that a conviction for smuggling would be -- could be accepted on the basis of this document. And of course -- but if you say, is the status only that Mr. Vasic denies being a smuggler, and I'm just taking this as an example, of course it would have two elements. First, Mr. Vasic testifying under oath, solemn declaration, denying it, and an unclear document, unclear to its sources, unclear as to its author, et cetera, saying that he or those he associated with were involved in smuggling. I hope by this explanation that you understand the formal status might be something quite different from what weight really to attach to such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until -- will 20 minutes do, Mr. Registrar? 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. At the same time, I already draw the attention of the parties to the blacklist. Since the common position seems to provide for a solution to the extent that the measures taken, in paragraph 1, "shall be without prejudice to the cases where a member state is bound by an obligation of international law, namely, number 1, as a host country of an international intergovernmental organisation." I don't know whether we are an international intergovernmental organisation, but at least it seems that due attention is paid to international obligations stemming from other sources than the common position taken by the EU.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, if Your Honour doesn't know that, I certainly don't, and I mean that with the greatest of respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But it seems to me that the blacklist is not intended to serve as an obstacle to fulfilling its obligations toward international organisations and their organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, moving to a different subject: You indicated that you didn't know about or were not familiar with any strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb political authorities or people. This Court has received evidence that on the 14th of May, the presidents of Kljuc, Sipovo, Mrkonjic Grad, Jajce, Donji Vakuf, Bugojno had a meeting with military officials within that area of responsibility, at which, among other things, the strategic goals which had been promulgated at the 16th Assembly Session two days earlier were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, that's P244 and also P529 in evidence. It's also tab 35 in these materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, are you saying there was no similar contact between military officials in your area of responsibility and the political officials in your area concerning the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any meetings with the military leadership, and no aims or goals were being looked into or -- I mean, I can claim upon my full responsibility that there were no meetings of that sort in our area, and I've already said everything I can say about this document, because I've never set eyes on him. And we had a very bad relationship with the military. Three or four presidents had been arrested and then released. They were a state within a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You never set eyes on a document reflecting the strategic goals; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was really surprised to have seen it here for the first time. I'd never seen it before. Let me not repeat who I was and what I did. As the president of the municipality, I can claim that there were no meetings of that sort, nothing where this document would have been presented. I had never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen it, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just stopped you because you had answered the question and then you were going on.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You know, that document was published in the Official Gazette. How did you miss it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must have missed it, but I can't believe it was published. I know that I'm speaking under oath, and I can tell you that I've never seen it, either in the Official Gazette or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, irrespective of whether you saw a specific document listing the strategic goals, you were aware of at least a number of the goals of the Bosnian Serb authorities and military organs, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ones that were presented publicly at meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, you knew that one of the goals was the establishment of a corridor linking the Krajina to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic goal was for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia together with Serbia. That was the goal and the wish. And as to your question, it is normal that the goal for the corridor was that. Because we were terribly frightened, since we had been cut off from our mother state, which was very important for the Serb people then, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Mr. Tieger did not ask you what was the rationale for a corridor. His question simply was whether you knew that one of the goals was the establishment of a corridor linking the Krajina to Serbia. May I take it from your answer that you were aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was the goal, the general, overall goal within the people. And as to whether it was a strategic goal, I don't know. I had never seen that document and I don't know what goals were listed there. Don't catch me in a trap of misunderstanding once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not catching you in a trap. I'm inviting you to answer the questions rather than to explain a lot of other things. If what you're saying is that the corridor could be an important element for not losing touch between Bosnia and Serbia, but the question simply was whether you were aware that the establishment of the corridor was one of the strategic goals. And at least you understood how important it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not aware of it to be a strategic goal, but [Previous translation continues]... Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's not have any magic language here. Didn't you know that it was an important military goal and therefore a strategic goal in that sense?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went without saying that it was both a military and a strategic goal, but not in the sense of any strategic goals, any purported strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And didn't you know that another goal was a unified state and contiguous territory so that the Serbs wouldn't be separated from one another by a border?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of the Serb population was that, yes. But you are trying to establish a link between myself and this document and strategic goals. It is still my desire, even today, but desires are one thing and political possibilities and politics are totally something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's not worry about what you think I'm trying to do. Let's just worry about what you knew. And so the answer is yes, you knew that it was a military objective, and in that sense, a strategic objective, of the Bosnian Serb forces to establish contiguous territory and prevent any border from separating the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also knew that one of the, if not the primary objective of the war was the establishment of a Serbian state and the ethnic division of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina into a Serbian state, and then -- where the Serbs would be, and then Muslim territory and Croat territory?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the variants that were being looked into at the time, at a higher level, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the primary focus, wasn't it, the creation of a Serbian state and the ethnic division of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina? It's not a hard question.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main aim was, if there was no other way, to have a peaceful separation, so to say, without any war. If we really didn't want to live together. And during talks amongst the three parties, attempts were made to negotiate that, and the war was not the goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on, in the interests of time. You also mentioned Variant A and B, the instructions of 19 December 1991, and indicated that you'd never heard of them, I think. Do you think that Dragan Djuric, for example, had ever heard of them? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen him before coming here. I've already mentioned that. It was shown to me by the Defence team for the first time. And at that meeting, I mean the Holiday Inn meeting, I attended the meeting, and it was not circulated to all the delegates and I didn't get a copy and I didn't hear about that having been discussed. As to whether Dragan Djuric had heard of it, had been given a copy or whatever, I do not know. Had he been given a copy, he would have been forwarded -- he would have forwarded it to us, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because, as you indicated to Dr. Karadzic, you usually communicated with the leadership through Dragan Djuric; right? Just referring to the telephone conversation we heard.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was a newly elected president, and it was just a matter of a couple of months, and for the first few months I communicated through him if there was anything to say. I didn't mean in terms of communication as such, but if we had some needs within our municipality, we would get him to get in touch. So, for example, when -- I mean, that was customary, to go through the local MP to get in touch with the top authorities. And so, for example, the time we wanted Mr. Karadzic to get Mr. -- General Talic, rather, to ask soldiers not to carry weapons in their home leave. So that was the sort of communication we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll just draw your attention quickly to late January 1991. Mr. Djuric attended the Bosnian Serb Assembly Session on the 26th of January, 1991, at which it was publicly stated, stated at that meeting, openly, by one of the persons present: "To solve this problem, I propose that we begin with an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out." Does that refresh your recollection about whether or not Mr. Djuric might have mentioned the instructions of 19 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that I had never seen it or heard about it before coming here. As to whether it was such a carefully kept secret for him not to mention it, I don't know, but I can honestly say that I had never either seen it or heard of it before coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I suggested to you the other day that you were an extremely loyal and indeed fervent supporter of Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, and you agreed that you thought highly of both men. But let me focus on a couple of examples of the extent of your commitment to the Bosnian Serb leadership. When Dr. Karadzic was removed from office, isn't it the case that you called the international community responsible for that the enemy?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, all that was misinterpreted in the media. I don't know exactly in what way it was interpreted here, because it was reported that I said that I was and remained a follower of Radovan Karadzic's and Momcilo Krajisnik's policies, and I said that I was and remain, and I still am, a supporter of the policies pursued by the Serb Democratic Party. And that in relation to Prnjavor, these two gentlemen were not to blame for anything, and if anything happened there, those of us at the local level would be to blame. I mean, I am not into idols, and other than God I'm not into worshipping anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the question was whether you referred to the international community responsible for Mr. Karadzic to be removed from office as the enemy. That's the question. Did you ever refer to the international community in this context as the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not within that context. Otherwise not either. I mean, that's not my usual vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said you're not into idols. Didn't you say that the removal of Dr. Karadzic had accelerated the process of creating a living saint?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And isn't it --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the opinion and the sentiment of the Serbian people, that he is a living saint. I believe you know what I'm trying to say, that when somebody's absent, he seems to be even more precious because there's some sort of a mystery enveloping the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, didn't you encourage people to meet illegally with this living saint, despite the actions that had been taken by the international community? Didn't you say to a crowd of supporters, "They can't prevent us from meeting illegally with him, receiving directions"?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life did I hear about his whereabouts, did I meet with him, or did I tell anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, again, Mr. Tieger asked you whether you ever said to a crowd of supporters, "They can't prevent us from meeting illegally with him, receiving directions." That's a simple question, not whether you knew where he was living, but whether you said that to a crowd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'd like the document found at tab 27, an article from the Moscow Times of July 26, 1996 marked and numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic -- I'm sorry. I should have waited for the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, P959 and the English translation P959.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vasic, I'll just bring to your attention, this is an article by journalist Christine Spolar following a rally in Prnjavor, and I'll simply note that the quotes that I asked you about are found in an article, in particular, the last comment that I asked you about is found on the second page of the article, indicating that you made those remarks to more than 300 applauding people. Do you recall that rally?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. It was a rally of the Serbian Democratic Party during the electoral campaign for the 1996 elections, I believe it was, the first postwar elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also the case that --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more than 300 persons present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps first the question and the last line, does that reflect what you said? On from "they can't prevent us from meeting illegally."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last paragraph, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what -- what's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is, if you look at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke at this electoral rally during the electoral campaign, at the time when Karadzic was still at large, and there were no measures in place at the time, as there do exist today by the ICTY to the effect that one can't meet with him or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this question simply is whether this reflects what you said, not whether you were entitled to say it, not whether it was -- well, whatever. The simple question: Is this what you said, as reported in the Moscow Times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With hindsight, I cannot claim not to have said so, but since I don't remember, I will say that I did not, although it is possible that I did say that, because it wasn't illegal at the time, because the man was still at large, he was meeting with other officials and public figures, and that's why I find it hard to grasp why I would have said that at the time in the first place. Since I do not remember, to be on the safe side, I will say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. You've got two minutes left. I take it that we finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Didn't you also anticipate a time when Dr. Karadzic and Mr. -- and General Mladic would need to hide, and didn't you offer them refuge in Prnjavor by saying: "If you are in trouble, you should know where to come, to a place where there is an army and a people who will be able and know how to protect both themselves and you"? This is at a different rally. Or maybe the same rally, pardon me, but this is at a rally for Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that. Many different things are said at rallies in order to score votes. I don't remember whether I said this or not, but I wish to point out that in this period, the man was still free to move around and meet with public figures. I have a different opinion today, however. I believe that they should appear before the Tribunal and prove their innocence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have that on video, Mr. Vasic. If you'll take my word for it and trust the translation, it won't be necessary to play it. Of course, I'm prepared to do so if you find that necessary, but in light of your answer, I thought not.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, because I said that this was uttered in the context of an electoral rally, where -- prompted by the national euphoria, might have uttered those words, but I did also say that at that time the man was still free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you said: "I don't recall saying that." And then you explained in your first answer that if you would have said it, it would have been under those circumstances. In your last answer, you said: "I don't think it's necessary," that's to play the video, "because I said that this was uttered in the context of an electoral rally," which seems to say that you do remember you said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Prosecutor asked me whether I trusted him and whether there was any need for him to show it to me, and I believe that the OTP is not given to producing fabrications. I do trust them, and I said that I do not remember, but if the video shows the contrary, then I must have said it but forgot. But I also wanted to provide an explanation as to the time in which these things took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're running out of time at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd offer the video in evidence, and then I have one additional question and that would conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Your Honour says anything, unsurprisingly I now have about a 15-minute re-examination. The witness has been cross-examined for what, two and a half days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You will start re-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Oh, tomorrow. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no way, Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I feel even a little bit embarrassed that you had the impression that -- first of all, we usually stop at a quarter to 2.00, but apart from that, I'm really a bit embarrassed by even the idea that we would say, well, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour will remember, I made that offer when we were last in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in the present circumstances, I would not hold it against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, one little question: Your return has not been scheduled for today, has it? It has not been -- your return has not been scheduled for today, has it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was scheduled for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the second half --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would find it very important to fly out tomorrow, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what time is your flight scheduled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I have a flight scheduled at about 12.00. I believe I have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any later flight tomorrow? We'll deal with that outside of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there are none. This is the only flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I do understand that you would prefer to fly back tomorrow. Nevertheless, this Court might insist --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- also in respect of the rights of the Defence, that at least some additional time would be available, both for questions of the Judges and of the Defence, and we'll see how to schedule that. We'll even look at possibilities this afternoon. I don't know, Mr. Tieger, whether that would at all be possible, as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're flexible and amenable to whatever suggestion the Court has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm available, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see, Mr. Vasic, to what extent we can meet your wish to fly back tomorrow morning. If not, we'll have to try to seek further arrangements for the re-examination and the questions of the Judges. It would certainly help if you would start answering the questions instead of giving explanations on matters unrelated, at least not directly related to the question. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber would like to see, once we resume, the video. It's not only offered, but we'd like to see it. Last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I just wanted to note that the Court had asked earlier for the OHR decision. We have that and can tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's located in tab 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's located in tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik had said some time ago that he was anxious to see the video. I know Your Honour said the Chamber wants to see it. I don't know whether there's any chance of him seeing it advance of the witness tomorrow. Perhaps that's something I could discuss with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just informed that we could continue until 2.30, but that would most likely not meet the time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you're not strongly opposing, the Chamber would like to give it a try to see how far we come in the next 40 minutes. I'll use as little words as possible. Mr. Tieger, did you have any -- was there any additional question or did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would play the video now. And then, Mr. Josse, if you would re-examine the witness. Let's, then, play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do understand that we need -- at least we could play the video, but we still need the consent of the head of the department of the interpreters. So let's see whether we get it. Otherwise we would have to stop and have to find other solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the benefit of the interpreters, they'll find the interpretation beginning on the second page, which is headed chapter 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]... President Karadzic, General Mladic, the black sheep of the Brankovic historical Serbian traitor, in this area, and therefore, if you're in trouble you should know where to come - to a place where there is an army and a people who will be able and know how to protect both themselves and you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we had some problems as far as the translation is concerned. Of course, we were able to read the translation. It's not on the transcript. There are other technical ways of getting it into the transcript, either by reading it in at a later stage or by referring to it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I welcome the Court's suggestion. I trust the Defence has no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, there's no trouble with that. Mr. Krajisnik is anxious to scrutinise the whole video. Could I just ask him in private why? Because it may be that's something I'm going to need to deal with with Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is that the video recording, the video footage, that the Prosecutor was putting questions to me about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the footage we were talking about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question about giving a place where there's an army to protect was taken from this video, so to that extent, the question of Mr. Tieger seems to be related to this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Vasic's question is whether I had additional areas of inquiry about that rally, of course the answer is no. I simply asked about whether that last statement was made and that's in fact even the portion we heard translated in English. So for the witness's benefit, it was just a question about that one comment that is reflected in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, my position is that in due course, I would ask the Prosecution to make the video available to the Defence in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the video in its entirety as we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not played in full, but I do understand that the transcript is the transcript of the full video. That's at least the position of the Prosecution. But I do understand that Mr. Krajisnik might not have seen now the whole of it. That might be a problem. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this was the rally in Prnjavor, not at Vucjak. This was the electoral rally in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to me there's no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there is no mention of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were two questions. One was the international community as the enemy. That's one. And then another question was put to you in relation to, well, giving a safe place for those who would need it. I have not understood that the Prosecution claimed it to be the same rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. This is what was said. If you find it hard to be on your own, you have a place to turn to. But there was no mention of them being chased after and us offering them shelter at that period in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Vasic, it suggests that it's of any relevance that there was an army to protect them. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just again ask the Prosecution the date of the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm only able to contextually date it based on a comment in the course of the video, after four years of war, but that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness said something about elections in 1996, or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I perhaps begin my re-examination this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help us with the date that you made that speech, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the electoral campaign for the 1996 elections. Therefore, it must have been sometime in summer 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at tab 27. In the report from the Moscow Times.com there are various quotations from a speech that you made at Prnjavor. Are you able to tell us: Is that a different speech, the one we saw you make on the video, the same speech, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is a speech delivered at Vucjak, at a pre-election rally there. And the one we saw on video was in Prnjavor, which was the very end of the pre-election campaign, and it took place after the one that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any leaders of the SDS present at the speech that you made on the video, the later one, in other words?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection, but it is only normal for them to be at the central meeting, since there were representatives at Vucjak also, somewhat lower-ranking. And therefore, it simply could not have happened for no one to attend that central meeting. According to the speech, on the basis of the speech, I would say that Karadzic himself was present, because since I am addressing him, in case you're in trouble, I suppose he must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at tab 26. That shows a photograph of Mr. Krajisnik making a speech. Where did he make that speech, please?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a pre-election rally at Vucjak, describing the document that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that document already got a number? 26? It's an existing exhibit. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about that speech that Mr. Krajisnik made at Vucjak. He makes reference to the Wolves of Vucjak, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could read the journalist's text first, because I can't remember. Yes, the last sentence by Mr. Krajisnik: "We were Wolves and we shall remain Wolves, for all those who want to snatch away our freedom and the Republika Srpska from our people."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've already told us this was at an electoral rally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you discuss the Wolves of Vucjak with Mr. Krajisnik prior to his making this speech?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There was no need to discuss them, because it was common knowledge. Perhaps we might have commented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the reference at tab 27 to your speech, are you able to tell us whether that was the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At tab 27, the reference is to the speech from the rally in Banja Luka. Oh, no, sorry. I do apologise. Not in Banja Luka; at Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one further point on this. Let's be fair to the Moscow Times. It's Moscow Times, not a local paper. How far is Vucjak from Prnjavor distance-wise?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the video is concerned, you've told us that it was an election speech. Just remind us: What position were you standing for?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a candidate as an MP for the Assembly of the Republic, the Republic of Srpska, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were you elected?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there anything else about the video you'd like to tell us?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, except that it was pre-election rally and the tensions normally mount. And on the basis of the speeches delivered, in order to win votes, I didn't say that we would be their shelter; we just said that you have the people and the army, as throughout the war, Prnjavor was well known for good and strong armed forces and that's why we had as many as 540 fallen fighters and that's why there were almost no Wolves left, because most of them were killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to move on to a different topic, and that is the documents that you brought to the Court with you. You've explained that the letter from the VWU you only received when you arrived at your hotel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the Tribunal official.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, there are two different issues here. Firstly, as a result of that letter, what did you do to try and obtain the information contained within it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rang a friend in Prnjavor and asked him to get in touch with the municipal secretary, somebody who was there when I was there, and to fax me the minutes from the Assembly meetings and the attendance lists, and I asked him to go to Merhamet to see whether they had any copies of letters, including the lists of Muslims who, back in 1992, 1993, and 1994, applied to leave through the Red Cross, the lists that would have been submitted to the Red Cross, and if possible, to fax all that through as soon as possible, and at any rate, by 9.00 a.m. this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I just consulted with my colleagues. The matter of what happened exactly not fully correct or correct, et cetera, is not something that's bothering the Chamber very much. Of course, in the questions this morning, we'd like to have clear answers on some matters, but we are not -- don't consider it to be of dramatic dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words, in relation to this witness's testimony in general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if there's any specific issue you would like to raise with him, fine, but the events we talked about are not determinative for the Chamber, although perhaps not agreeing with the way it happened, does not necessarily explain it as some intelligent way of trying to deceive whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very helpful. Could I just make this comment, really, and I address this to my learned friends through Your Honour: It was the Prosecution who wanted this witness to produce these documents, the ones I'm referring to, in other words, the ones that have been faxed to him this morning. I assume they have received them and I assume they have chosen not to cross-examine upon them, either because they haven't had a chance to have them translated or because -- I just want to be clear about this, because I'm not going to ask any questions about these documents, because could I emphasise again, it was the Prosecution who asked Mr. Vasic to obtain them, in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Counsel is quite right. It was really no decision to be made because there was really no opportunity to either examine the documents, or had there been such opportunity, there was no translation facility available either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we agree that at this moment, there was no real opportunity for the Prosecution to do so. I also do understand that at this moment there's no claim for recalling the witness on the basis of an unknown document yet. May I also understand, and I'm just thinking on what I would do under similar circumstances, that is to reserve the right to use those documents at a later stage properly introduced through other witnesses, through other means, whatever, but that the Prosecution does not give up its right to ever use the documents? Is that a correct assumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Court anticipated precisely the only position we could take under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, you can act on the basis of this assumption. It's now confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to turn immediately to the other documents, the documents that you handed to Mr. Divcic. Have you got those there, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. You, for better or for worse, brought those along to this Court on this, your second visit to The Hague; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want you to briefly explain why. Let's go through them document by document. Firstly, we have the document which looks like a certificate in Cyrillic, dated the 24th of March, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the Court have copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have copies. We received copies of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've got the original there, I see. What is it? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly what it is.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the highest honour that the Municipal Assembly of Prnjavor can award, and it is normally awarded on the day of the municipality. This is called the charter of respected citizen for the municipality of Prnjavor, and of a worthy citizen, and there is a coat of arms of the municipality, and I'm the only one who has been awarded this so far. And it says the reason just below my name. It says: "For exceptional contribution to the maintenance of peace and stability, as well as the development of the municipality of Prnjavor."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And which body in Prnjavor awarded this to you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prnjavor Municipal Assembly awarded it to me; therefore, the highest body of authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on: You have produced various letters, some in English, some in B/C/S, from the OSCE and from the OHR. Why did you produce those, please?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document indicates that Prnjavor municipality essentially completed the application of property-related laws. It was therefore the first municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina which essentially completed the application of the property-related laws, which means that in Prnjavor, these matters operate precisely as indicated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
